summary: Short recap: review of 2027-02-15 incident where tail latency spike caused request timeouts for Lynx's fraud-detection pipeline. Root cause: cold KV-cache population combined with autoscaler thresholds and a model fallback path that retried to a heavyweight variant. Agreed mitigations: prefix caching warmup, autoscaler tuning, circuit breaker on fallbacks, add Dedicated warm pools for peak windows, and schedule a production replay run.
topics: Long-term reliability improvements (warm pools, circuit breakers)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Length: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Iris Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Rivera (Redwood CSM), Maya Rodriguez (Lynx SRE), Ethan Cole (Lynx Head of Platform), Priya Sharma (Lynx CTO)
Shared artifacts: Lynx incident postmortem draft (https://redwood.app/postmortems/lynx-2027-02), benchmark spreadsheet (shared), logs bundle link (s3://lynx-incident-2027-02)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a quick postmortem review, root cause and then walk through mitigations. Diego and Iris from our side, Maya, Ethan, Priya from Lynx. Can we confirm agenda?
[00:12] Priya: Yep, that's good. we want clear owners and dates. the outage cost us a few hours of delayed fraud alerts so.. urgency is high.
[00:20] Maya: I can run through the timeline and what we observed in the logs, that might help.
[00:25] Iris: Perfect. I'll also summarize what we changed on the platform during the incident and proposed longer-term fixes.

--- Summary of the incident / timeline ---
[02:05] Maya: On 2027-02-15 at 02:14 UTC we started seeing elevated p95 and p99 latencies from the redwood inference endpoints used by our streaming fraud pipeline. Over 18 minutes we had progressive timeouts, total of ~1,600 requests failed or retried. We saw a pattern: a large batch of new session keys caused the KV cahce to get lots of cold misses, combined with autoscaler not spinning up fast enough. Some requests then retried to the heavier model variant and that amplified queued work.
[03:10] Ethan: The spike coincided with a nightly batch job from our onboarding system, we didn't realize it would fan out to realtime inference.
[03:35] Samir: To be clear, the immediate root cause was a combination of cold KV cache population and autoscaler thresholds being too conservative, plus retry/fallback behavior — Iris?
[03:48] Iris: Right. Also a config detail: the fallback model had a larger context window and used a different kernel path, which increased resource usage per token. The system lacked a circuit breaker to stop cascading retries.

--- Imperfect transcription / side notes ---
[05:00] Maya: there were also some 403s around KMS during rotation - I think some keys were briefly unavailable, that caused a small subset of requests to fail. maybe unrelated, maybe just coincident.
[05:18] Diego: We saw an alert for KMS latency, but the majority of errors were timeouts before KMS returned. we'll investigate the key rotation overlap.

--- Mitigations applied during incident ---
[07:00] Iris: During the incident we throttled the onboarding fan-out, adjusted scaling policy temporary (reduced the CPU/queue threshold to spin up pods earlier), and disabled the heavyweight fallback by returning an error instead of retrying. That reduced the tail and brought p99 back down in about 10 minutes.
[07:38] Samir: We also enabled additional logging for KV hot keys and increased cache capacity for the affected pool.

--- Discussion: Long-term fixes ---
[09:20] Priya: What's in the long-term roadmap? we need SLAs.
[09:27] Iris: Three pillars: 1) Warm pools / Dedicated reserved capacity for your peak windows so cold-starts are minimized. 2) Autoscaler improvements: predictive warmup for known batch windows plus smoothing on the trigger thresholds. 3) Failure isolation: circuit breakers and throttling on fallback paths + per-route concurrency limits.
[10:05] Maya: Warm pools sound good. can we guarantee they won't be reclaimed? we need isolation during our scheduled jobs.
[10:12] Samir: For Dedicated pools we can offer pinning and pre-warm options. they'll be reserved and won't be reaped under normal reclaim cycles. There's a pricing delta which I'll share.
[10:40] Ethan: Also want better telemetry — token-level latency breakdowns and KV cache hit rates per route.
[10:48] Iris: We'll add per-route dashboards in Console and export a CSV for your team with token latency, cache hit ratio, model variant usage.

--- Security & compliance discussion ---
[12:20] Priya: Maya mentioned KMS rotation noise. we need to confirm audit logs and whether the rotation could have caused short-lived permission denials.
[12:33] Diego: I'll open a support ticket and validate the rotation window. we also have audit logs and SAML/SSO traces.
[12:45] Maya: From our side we rotate keys at 02:00 UTC weekly; this was at 02:05 that day and overlapped with onboarding.
[13:00] Samir: Action: Diego will validate KMS integration and provide evidence that rotation didn't leave any persistent permissions gap.

--- Objections and tradeoffs ---
[15:00] Ethan: If we move to Dedicated warm pools, cost goes up. we need to see a cost/benefit.
[15:08] Samir: Understood — Redwood Optimize can run a cost simulation using your traffic profile and show delta between hosted autoscale vs Dedicated reserved capacity with warm pools and caching. I'll include that in the pricing packet.
[15:35] Priya: What's the risk if we only tune autoscaler and don't pay for Dedicated?
[15:42] Iris: Tuning helps reduce probability but doesn't remove cold-start risk for extreme fan-outs. Dedicated warm pools are the most robust for critical pipelines. There's also an option for scheduled pre-warm: spin up at known windows cheaper than full reservation.

--- Technical deep-dive snippets ---
[18:10] Iris: On the runtime side, we saw two things: (1) KV cache had many cold misses for new user sessions, increasing per-request latency; (2) the fallback variant triggered a heavy kernel path with larger attention and dequantized ops. That doubled tokens/sec work for those requests. Without circuit breaker the queued requests stacked.
[19:05] Maya: Any quick fixes we should do?
[19:12] Iris: Immediate: adjust autoscale policy to lower target CPU threshold from 70% to 55% for the affected route, implement a soft throttle on retries, and add a simple circuit-breaker that returns a 429 when queue depth crosses threshold. Long-term: prefix warm caching and reserved warm vector store for first 100k keys during batch windows.

--- Shared artifacts and references ---
[22:00] Samir: link to the draft postmortem: https://redwood.app/postmortems/lynx-2027-02 - please comment, we'll incorporate your timeline. Also benchmark sheet: https://sheets.redwood/apps/lynx-bench-2027 (contains replay results and model latency curves).
[22:20] Ethan: We'll upload anonymized replay data to s3 and share the path.

--- Questions from customer ---
[25:00] Maya: Will the circuit breaker affect accuracy? returning 429 might drop events in window. can we queue instead?
[25:10] Iris: Queueing exacerbates tail latency; for critical fraud detection dropping low-confidence events or sampling is safer than cascading timeouts. We can implement a graceful degradation mode: return a lightweight scoring path (approximate model) instead of full model. That preserves processing while reducing load.
[26:05] Priya: Can Redwood guarantee audit logs for every reroute/fallback for compliance?
[26:12] Diego: Yes, Console can provide audit trail per request including model variant and fallback reasons. We'll map it to your compliance templates.

--- Recap and owners ---
[30:00] Samir: Quick recap: Iris + Diego produce mitigation runbook with exact config changes and rollback steps; Samir shares Dedicated pricing and cost simulation; Maya to provide replay dataset; Redwood to run a replay in staging and share results.
[30:25] Priya: We want a dry-run of scheduled pre-warm and autoscaler changes in staging before production.
[30:33] Iris: Agreed — we'll coordinate dates.

--- Wrap-up ---
[45:00] Ethan: Thanks, appreciate the quick response.
[45:05] Maya: yeah thanks. we'll review the postmortem draft this afternoon.
[45:12] Samir: I'll send meeting notes and action items. Next checkpoint: Dedicated capacity plan review next Thursday, 2027-02-25.
[45:20] Diego: I'll open the support ticket for KMS and share ticket number.

(Transcription ends)

Notes on transcription quality: some acronyms were mis-recognized ("KV cahce" -> KV cache, "KMS" sometimes overlapped with timing), speaker labels may be slightly off in places.
